lesson.title: When Two Chances Multiply
lesson.objective: Recognize independent events and compute the probability that both happen using the multiplication rule.
lesson.approachReason: The learner first predicts and counts joint outcomes, then tests whether one event changes another event's probability before applying the multiplication rule.

blocks.heading: Why multiplication works
blocks.body:
The eight equally likely outcomes are heads–blue, heads–red, heads–green, heads–yellow, and the same four colors paired with tails. Only heads–blue gives both successes.

The coin and spinner are independent: knowing the coin result does not change the probability of any spinner result. Half the outcomes have heads, and one quarter of those also have blue, so P(heads and blue) = 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

For independent events A and B, the multiplication rule is P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Here, “and” means both events happen.
blocks.example: Think of taking a fraction of a fraction: one quarter of the heads outcomes, not one quarter plus one half.

hints: You need both successes, not either success.
The events are independent, so multiply their probabilities.
blocks.retry: Keep only the coin outcomes with heads. Within that half, only one third of the spinner outcomes show a star.

blocks.heading: Check independence before multiplying
blocks.body:
Independent does not just mean “two different events.” It means that learning one event happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged.

In a bag with one red ball and one blue ball, the first draw has a 1/2 chance of red. If you keep a red ball out, the second draw cannot be red; if you return it and mix thoroughly, the second draw still has a 1/2 chance of red.

Multiply the two original probabilities only when the events are independent. Without independence, that shortcut can give the wrong answer.

hints: What remains in the bag after a red ball is drawn?
Can both draws be red if the bag contains only one red ball?
blocks.retry: Imagine the first draw really is red. There is now only a blue ball left, so a second red is impossible.

blocks.heading: Apply it in a new setting
blocks.prompt:
In a fictional delivery model, a parcel passes through two checkpoints. It has a 0.8 probability of clearing the first checkpoint on time and a 0.9 probability of clearing the second on time. The model states that these events are independent.

What is the probability that the parcel clears both checkpoints on time? Enter a decimal.

traps.feedback: You added the probabilities. For both independent events to happen, multiply instead.
This accounts for only the first checkpoint. Some parcels that clear it will not clear the second on time.

hints: The model explicitly gives independence, so the multiplication rule applies.
Multiply 8/10 by 9/10, then write the result as a decimal.
blocks.solution: Because the events are independent, multiply: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72. The probability of clearing both checkpoints on time is 0.72.

activities.title: Heads and blue
activities.prompt: You flip a fair coin and spin a fair spinner with four equal sections: blue, red, green, and yellow. The coin result does not affect the spinner. What is the probability of getting heads AND blue?
activities.reveal: Pair each coin result with each of the four colors: there are eight equally likely pairs. Just one pair is heads–blue, so the probability is 1/8.

options.feedback: That is the probability of blue alone. You also need heads.
That is the probability of heads alone. You also need blue.
Exactly: one of the eight equally likely coin–color pairs gives both.
Adding 1/2 and 1/4 does not count the outcomes where both happen.

activities.title: Unchanged or changed?
activities.prompt: For each experiment, compare the second event's probability before and after learning that the first event happened. Drag it into the matching group.
activities.reveal: Returning a ball restores the original chances; keeping it out changes what is available. Independence is about unchanged probabilities, not whether the events use the same object.

items.text: Two independent fair coin flips: after learning that the first is heads, what is the chance the second is heads?
A bag has one red and one blue ball. Draw randomly, return the ball, and mix thoroughly. After learning that the first draw was red, what is the chance the second is red?
A bag has one red and one blue ball. Draw randomly and keep the ball out. After learning that the first draw was red, what is the chance the second is red?
A bag has one red and one blue ball. Draw randomly and keep the ball out. After learning that the first draw was blue, what is the chance the second is red?

questions.question: A game uses a fair coin and an independent fair spinner with three equal sections, exactly one marked with a star. You win only if you get heads and the star. What is your probability of winning?
questions.explanation: The events are independent, so P(heads and star) = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

questions.question: A bag contains one red ball and one blue ball. You draw both balls, one at a time, without returning the first. A friend claims the probability of two reds is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Which response is correct?
options: The answer is 1/4 because there are two draws.
The answer is 0 because drawing red first leaves no red ball for the second draw.
The answer is 1/2 because the first draw has a 1/2 chance of red.
The answer is 1 because drawing both balls guarantees two reds.
questions.correctAnswer: The answer is 0 because drawing red first leaves no red ball for the second draw.
questions.explanation: Two reds are impossible because there is only one red ball. The draws are not independent, so multiplying their original probabilities gives the wrong result.
